data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A large service with strictly more total internal redundancy is more resilient to correlated failure than a decentralized network of small services, provided the large service has the resources to diversity its redundant components across independent supply chains, geographies, and software implementations. The problem's premise that the large service has 'strictly more total internal redundancy' implies it can afford redundancy in the dimensions that matter for correlation, while small services cannot.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the large service's redundancy is strictly homogeneous (e.g., many copies of the same software on the same hardware), the claim fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the small services, through coordination, achieve diversity along the relevant dimensions (e.g., a protocol that requires diverse implementations), the claim weakens.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Correlated failure is a function of shared dependencies. The large service, having more redundancy, can diversify not only the number of components but the *kinds* of components, supply chains, and operational procedures. A small service has fewer resources and cannot afford this diversity; it has a single stack, a single provider, a single team. The large service can engineer independence along the dimensions that would otherwise be shared causes; the small services have independence along dimensions that do not matter (e.g., ownership) but dependence along dimensions that do (e.g., infrastructure).","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
